title: Giao Tiếp Thông Minh (best-guess identification: Vietnamese translation of *How to Talk to Anyone: How to Charm, Banter, Attract, & Captivate*)
author: Patrick King (best-guess identification — see note below)
summary:
Giao Tiếp Thông Minh, based on its Vietnamese publisher description, is presented as a practical social-skills guide by Patrick King, an internationally bestselling author and self-described former shy introvert who built a career reverse-engineering conversation and social connection into a learnable, almost scientific skill. The book's promise, per its own marketing copy, is to help readers move past small talk into "smart" conversation — knowing what to say and when, in order to be liked, to connect, and to leave a memorable impression, across situations ranging from casual greetings to disagreement, sincere personal conversation, graceful farewells, and even defusing hostility or holding one's own in an argument.

Because I was not able to independently verify the book's exact original English title, full chapter list, or specific worked examples with confidence — and because this Vietnamese title closely overlaps with at least two other distinct books by different authors — I want to be direct about the limits of this entry. Patrick King's broader body of work (including *How to Talk to Anyone*, *Better Small Talk*, and *Read People Like a Book*) consistently emphasizes conversational technique broken into concrete, practicable moves: opening lines that avoid generic small talk, follow-up questions that deepen rather than stall a conversation, reading and responding to another person's conversational energy, and specific scripts for common social friction points like disagreement or an awkward exit.

Given the genuine ambiguity in exactly which King title this Vietnamese edition maps to, and the risk of blending content from several similarly structured books, I have kept the chapter-level detail below intentionally general rather than presenting invented, specific chapter content as if verified. The overall thrust of the book, consistent across King's related titles, is that social confidence and likability are built from a specific, learnable toolkit of conversational habits rather than an innate personality trait — an encouraging premise for socially anxious readers, delivered in a brisk, tip-driven style typical of King's catalog.

I'd recommend treating the summary and lessons below as representative of Patrick King's general approach to this topic rather than as a verified chapter-by-chapter account of this specific title, and flag that a stronger identification (ISBN, publisher, page count) would let me produce a more precise entry.

sections.title: Rethinking Small Talk
sections.summary:
This section reframes small talk not as meaningless filler but as the necessary on-ramp to any deeper conversation, and addresses why many people (including previously shy readers like the author himself) find it uncomfortable or pointless.

The chapter offers specific alternatives to generic opening lines, encouraging questions that invite a real, specific answer rather than a closed one, and framing the goal of early conversation as finding a genuine point of shared interest quickly rather than performing pleasantries.
keyLessons: Small talk functions as a necessary bridge to deeper conversation, not an end in itself.
Specific, open questions generate more usable conversational material than generic ones.

sections.title: Deepening the Conversation
sections.summary:
This section covers the transition from surface-level exchange into more substantive or personal territory, focused on follow-up questions and active listening as the primary tools for this shift.

The chapter emphasizes genuine curiosity and building on what the other person has already said, rather than redirecting the conversation back to yourself, as the key mechanism for making someone feel heard and interested in continuing to talk.
keyLessons: Following up on details the other person has already shared signals genuine interest more than introducing new topics.
Redirecting conversation back to yourself too often undermines connection, even unintentionally.

sections.title: Handling Disagreement and Difficult Moments
sections.summary: This section addresses conversational friction directly — disagreement, awkward silences, and hostile or dismissive responses — offering scripts and reframes for staying engaged without either backing down unnecessarily or escalating conflict.
keyLessons: Disagreement can be handled directly without it derailing the relationship, using specific de-escalating language.
Awkward silences are often less damaging than the anxious reaction to them; a calm pause can be reframed as natural.

sections.title: Ending Conversations Gracefully
sections.summary: This section covers a frequently overlooked skill: exiting a conversation smoothly and warmly, without abruptness or awkward lingering, which the book treats as equally important to starting one well.
keyLessons: A graceful exit leaves as strong an impression as a strong opening.
Clear, warm closing language avoids the discomfort of a conversation that trails off unresolved.
Small talk is a functional bridge to deeper conversation, not something to be dismissed or skipped.
Specific, open-ended questions generate more usable conversational material than generic ones.
Following up on details someone has already shared signals genuine interest more effectively than changing topics.
Disagreement can be navigated directly, without either capitulating or escalating, using specific reframing language.
A graceful, warm way of ending a conversation is as important to a positive impression as how it begins.
Conversational skill is a learnable, practicable toolkit, not a fixed personality trait.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Conversational Threading
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A general technique (consistent across Patrick King's related titles) of picking up specific details the other person has already mentioned and asking a follow-up question about them, rather than introducing unrelated new topics, in order to build depth and signal genuine attention.

actionSteps: In your next casual conversation, replace one generic opening question ("How are you?") with a specific, open one tied to something you can actually observe or know about the situation.

Practice conversational threading: in your next few conversations, deliberately ask at least one follow-up question that builds directly on something the other person just said, rather than introducing a new topic.
Prepare one calm, non-escalating script for disagreement ("I see it differently — can I share why?") and use it deliberately the next time you disagree with someone in conversation.
reflectionQuestions: Where do your conversations tend to stall — at the opening, in the middle, or when it's time to end them?
Do you tend to redirect conversations back toward yourself more than you realize?

points: The strongest limitation of this specific entry is identification uncertainty itself: at least three distinct books share this or a near-identical Vietnamese title, and I was not able to confirm with confidence which one corresponds to the physical book in the library.

Patrick King's broader catalog (dozens of similarly themed, independently published titles) is known for a brisk, tip-list style rather than deep theoretical or research-driven treatment, so readers seeking an evidence-based academic treatment of communication psychology may find it thin on citation and rigor.

Because King's books are independently published rather than backed by a traditional publisher's fact-checking process, claims presented as "science-based" in his marketing copy should be treated with some caution unless independently verified.

whoThisIsFor: Readers looking for a practical, tip-driven guide to everyday conversational confidence, assuming the identification above is correct.
whenToReadThis: Before a specific social situation you find anxiety-inducing (networking, dating, small talk with unfamiliar people), assuming the identification above is correct.

authorBio.name: Patrick King (best-guess identification)
authorBio.bio:
Patrick King is an internationally bestselling author and self-described social interaction specialist and coach, based in San Francisco, California, who has written extensively in the social skills and communication self-help space. According to his own author biography, he was a shy introvert for many years before developing and systematizing techniques for social confidence, which he now presents in his books and coaching work.

King has written a large number of titles in this space, generally independently published, covering conversation, body language, charisma, and reading other people, with a consistent style oriented toward brief, actionable techniques rather than extended theoretical discussion.
